analysis.title: Extremes II
key_insights: Thursday's NDX fell 6.36%, its worst day since Covid. Many GS AI-related baskets had their largest one-day drop since the ChatGPT launch. Friday brought some relief, but investors want to see Semis stabilize and would rather chase a breakout than buy into a choppy tape or dead-cat bounce.
The Democratic sweep in the midterms put heavier regulation of AI and data centers back on the table, and the AI sell-off came late in the week but was large.

Friday's payrolls came in at +165k vs about 65k expected. This eased the growth scare but pushed December hike odds to about 77%. Tuesday's CPI is the last before the December FOMC, and PPI and PCE still follow.
S&P ex AI was -0.3% on the week, while many prominent AI baskets fell 10% or more. Global AI stocks were the most sold in the past 5 years on a trailing 20-day basis.

Thursday market volume was 1.5x the prior 50-day average, matching or exceeding other large selling episodes over the past 5 years. It was the 4th largest volume day of the year, and by multiple of the 50-day average only Liberation Day was comparable.
Net selling of Tech (TMT + Communication Services) is above $30bn since the unwind began, versus $21bn in the July technical episode. Net selling this week was $6bn, concentrated in Tech.

Friday was the first Semi buy skew in 6+ sessions. HFs and long-only funds both net bought, +$1bn in Semis in total. HFs were 20% better to buy overall (+$4bn net), but about 90% of that was in macro products, so risk appetite into the weekend was low.
Hedge fund gross leverage ratio rose month/month because of mark-to-market. Gross market value fell sharply, but fund equity fell faster on performance losses (Vinny Lin).

Info Tech was the most net sold global and US sector this week. The percentage of selling in global Tech stocks was about on par with the largest net selling weeks on GS record (since 2016). HF selling of global AI stocks over 20 days was the largest in more than five years (-3.0 SD).
Top-of-book liquidity in E-mini S&P futures dropped as dealers pulled back during the sell-off.

The GS Vol Panic Index rose about 5 points to 9.57 out of 10 on Thursday, back in the panic zone (9.5+). It was the 3rd largest daily jump ever, after Wednesday's 4th largest drop ever. The combined two-day swing was the largest on record (Coppersmith).

Levered/inverse ETFs hold $140bn AUM, equal to $345bn gross exposure, below the June peaks. Participation hit new highs, with SOXL and SOXS posting record volume days. Wednesday saw record inflows to levered ETFs and record outflows from inverse ETFs (Chris Lucas).
CTAs are in sell mode, with big supply for S&P in a flat tape. They are long $23bn S&P (71st percentile) and short $1bn NDX (35th percentile). The medium-term SPX pivot level is 7547.

Retail has been a smaller factor than headlines suggest. Retail bought consistently in prior weeks and sold heavily Thursday, then reversed midday, but has not been an impactful share of the tape this year.
S&P buyback demand is running at about $5bn a day, with 90% of corporates in the open window Monday. Week-to-date volume is 1.4x 2025 YTD ADTV, vs 0.6x last week.

Semis positioning has almost fully roundtripped in 2026. NVDA is barely up YTD and its RSI is at levels last seen during Liberation Day. NDX forward P/E is 18.4x, below its 5 and 10 year averages and the lowest since 2020.

Mag7 net length is still at the 87th percentile over 1 year and 93rd over 3 years. It was seen as the midterm winner because less compute build means higher pricing for scaled players, but that buying was short-lived and the group fell sharply Thursday.
Breadth (S&P names above the 50-day moving average) had its biggest one-day drop since August but is still about 3x the Sep 30 low of 20.8%.

sector_views.rationale: The desk reports heavy net selling and a roundtrip in Semi positioning. It says investors want to see Semis stabilize before playing offense and would rather chase a breakout than buy a dead-cat bounce.
